prosecution_strengths: Section 61-8-401 mandates 24 hours minimum jail for first offense, 7 days for second, 30 days for third — rigid floors that limit judicial discretion.
ACE (Alcohol Compliance Enforcement) compliance is monitored by MDT and tracked across counties for sentencing enhancement.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 10-year lookback — prior convictions outside the window cannot be used to elevate the current offense.
Question Intoxilyzer maintenance and calibration documentation — Montana requires strict procedural compliance.
Challenge the legality of the traffic stop or DUI checkpoint under Montana's strict stop-justification standards.
Rising blood alcohol defense — argue that BAC was below .08 at the actual time of driving.
ACE program and 24/7 sobriety alternatives provide non-incarceration paths for first-time offenders.
common_defenses: Improper stop — no reasonable suspicion under Montana law.
Faulty breath test — instrument malfunction or expired calibration.
Rising BAC — alcohol still being absorbed at time of driving.
Involuntary intoxication — unknowing consumption of intoxicating substance.

prosecution_strengths: Section 61-8-401(1) imposes 24 consecutive hours imprisonment as a mandatory floor — courts cannot suspend below this minimum.
defense_opportunities: Court may suspend all but 24 hours of the sentence, providing significant flexibility.
Probationary license available after 45 days, mitigating practical license-loss impact.
Challenge the 24-hour observation period before chemical testing.
Medical conditions (GERD, diabetes, low-carb diet) can produce false breath readings.
common_defenses: Improper FST administration — failure to follow NHTSA standards.
Lack of probable cause for arrest.
Chain of custody issues with blood samples or breath testing protocols.

prosecution_strengths: Fourth or subsequent DUI is a felony with up to 5 years imprisonment.
Vehicle forfeiture is possible for repeat offenders under Montana law.
Prior conviction records are easily authenticated and admitted.
24/7 sobriety program participation may be ordered as a release or sentence condition.
defense_opportunities: Attack validity of prior convictions taken without counsel or proper advisements.
Argue out-of-state priors do not qualify under Montana's prior DUI definition.
Negotiate for treatment court diversion, particularly for third offense.
common_defenses: Out-of-state offense does not qualify under Montana definition.
Standard DUI defenses with heightened importance for felony exposure.

prosecution_strengths: Section 61-8-401(1)(b)-(d) covers driving under the influence of any drug — including legal and prescription medications.
DRE 12-step evaluations have been accepted by Montana courts as reliable evidence.
Toxicology results showing controlled substance presence combined with driving behavior support impairment findings.
No per se drug limit, but officer observations and testing combine to prove impairment.
defense_opportunities: Without per se drug limits, prosecution must prove actual impairment — drug presence alone is insufficient.
Challenge DRE officer's training currency, certification, and adherence to the 12-step protocol.
Drug metabolites (especially THC) can persist for weeks without indicating current impairment.
Valid prescription defense for medications taken as directed at therapeutic levels.
common_defenses: Lack of impairment — metabolite presence does not prove impairment.
Flawed DRE evaluation — failure to follow protocol.
Alternative explanation — fatigue, medical condition, or illness.

prosecution_strengths: Section 61-8-301 requires only willful or wanton disregard for safety — a relatively easy mental state to establish.
Witness testimony, dashcam footage, and accident scene evidence demonstrate dangerous driving directly.
Prior traffic violations can support awareness of dangerous driving habits.
Officer testimony about driving observations is given significant weight.
defense_opportunities: First-offense maximum is only 90 days, providing room for diversion.
Common plea-down destination from DUI charges.
Challenge the 'willful or wanton' standard — argue ordinary negligence.
Emergency circumstances or sudden mechanical failure may explain the behavior.
common_defenses: Insufficient evidence of willful or wanton disregard.

prosecution_strengths: Section 61-7-103 requires stopping, providing identification, and rendering aid — failure on any element satisfies the offense.
Vehicle identification through paint transfer, debris, and surveillance footage frequently identifies the responsible vehicle.
Witness testimony combined with matching vehicle damage establishes the link.
Forensic accident reconstruction can determine the involved vehicle's characteristics.
defense_opportunities: Argue lack of knowledge that a collision occurred — viable for minor low-speed contacts.
Demonstrate the defendant returned to the scene or reported the accident promptly.
Challenge identification of the defendant's vehicle as the one involved.
Safety defense — defendant left briefly due to credible threat and reported promptly.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge of the collision.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-106 covers negligent vehicular assault and homicide — deaths caused by negligent vehicle operation.
Toxicology evidence in DUI-related fatal cases is devastating to the defense.
Accident reconstruction expert testimony establishes speed, failure to brake, and other negligent factors.
Victim impact testimony at sentencing carries substantial weight.
defense_opportunities: Challenge causation — intervening factors may break the causal chain.
Dispute accident reconstruction methodology through competing experts.
Argue mere negligence rather than the criminal negligence required.
Highlight comparative fault of the victim or third parties.
common_defenses: Intervening cause as actual proximate cause.
Lack of criminal negligence — conduct did not rise to gross deviation.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-104 covers negligent homicide caused by vehicle operation.
Recklessness shown through speed, intoxication, distracted driving, or aggressive maneuvers.
Physical evidence from the crash supports the negligent driving narrative.
Prior dangerous driving incidents may be admissible to show pattern.
defense_opportunities: Distinguish ordinary negligence from criminal negligence.
Sudden medical emergency defense (seizure, heart attack, syncope).
Mechanical failure — vehicle defect contributing to the collision.
Contributory fault of the victim.

prosecution_strengths: Proof of notice eliminates the lack of knowledge defense.
Officer testimony confirming operation of a vehicle is straightforward.
Repeat violations carry escalating penalties.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether actual notice was received — defective service or address errors.
Argue good-faith belief that the license had been reinstated.
Necessity defense for genuine emergencies.
First offense is a misdemeanor with limited penalties.
common_defenses: Mistaken identity — defendant was not the driver.

prosecution_strengths: Section 61-8-316 covers fleeing or eluding a peace officer with potential for felony enhancement.
Dashcam and patrol vehicle video clearly document pursuits.
Officer testimony about activated lights/sirens and failure to stop is direct evidence.
Reckless driving during the pursuit supports additional or enhanced charges.
defense_opportunities: Argue lack of awareness that a law enforcement vehicle was attempting a stop.
Challenge the lawfulness of the underlying stop — unlawful stops do not create a duty to stop.
Safety defense — defendant sought a well-lit, populated area before stopping.
Brief delay or hesitation may not constitute the offense.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge that officer was signaling.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-9-102 makes criminal possession of dangerous drugs a felony for most controlled substances.
Physical evidence plus lab confirmation creates a strong case.
Constructive possession doctrine allows conviction without drugs on the person.
Statements made to officers during the encounter may be admissible.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the search — Fourth Amendment violations result in suppression.
Constructive possession requires both knowledge and dominion/control — proximity is insufficient.
Treatment courts and deferred prosecution programs are available for many drug offenders.
Field test reliability challenges — false positives are documented.
common_defenses: Lack of possession — no actual or constructive control.

prosecution_strengths: Possession by minors or in restricted locations is still prosecutable.
Distribution-quantity possession can be charged regardless of legalization for personal amounts.
Public consumption violations remain enforceable.
defense_opportunities: Montana legalized recreational marijuana — possession of up to 1 ounce by adults 21+ is legal.
Medical marijuana patients have higher possession limits.
Weight disputes — challenge actual amount excluding stems and packaging.
Local ordinance challenges where jurisdictions attempt to override state legalization.
common_defenses: Weight dispute — usable amount below threshold.

prosecution_strengths: Lab confirmation of cocaine through chemical analysis is reliable.
Even residue amounts in paraphernalia can support possession charges.
Cocaine's association with distribution often triggers additional investigation.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the search and seizure — Fourth Amendment suppression eliminates physical evidence.
Drug treatment court eligibility provides diversion alternatives.
Constructive possession defense in shared spaces.
Field test challenges — cocaine field tests have known false positive rates.
common_defenses: Constructive possession failure — no link to defendant.
Lab analysis errors or chain of custody issues.

prosecution_strengths: Meth-related paraphernalia provides strong corroborating evidence.
Residue testing confirms methamphetamine presence even without usable quantity.
Montana has extensive meth enforcement infrastructure and experienced investigators.
defense_opportunities: Treatment courts in Montana specifically target meth offenders for treatment-based alternatives.
Constructive possession challenges in shared living situations.
Suppress evidence from warrantless searches.
Substance identification challenges — require lab confirmation rather than field tests.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge of substance nature.
Substance misidentification from unreliable field test.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-9-101 covers criminal distribution with severe penalties — life imprisonment possible for some substances.
Quantity-based charging is straightforward once drugs are seized and weighed.
Wiretap evidence, confidential informants, and surveillance commonly used.
Federal adoption of state cases brings even harsher mandatory minimums.
defense_opportunities: Challenge weight calculation — packaging and cutting agents may or may not be included.
Scrutinize confidential informant credibility, motives, and benefits received.
Challenge wiretap authorization for procedural compliance.
Mere presence is not participation.
common_defenses: Entrapment by law enforcement or informants.
Lack of knowledge of drugs' presence.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-9-101(1) covers distribution, delivery, and sale of dangerous drugs.
Controlled buy operations with audio/video recording provide strong direct evidence.
Text messages and electronic communications about transactions are admissible.
Distribution-indicative evidence (packaging, scales, cash) supports the charge.
defense_opportunities: Challenge confidential informant reliability — criminal history and incentives.
Personal use defense — quantity consistent with consumption.
Challenge controlled buy chain of custody and recording quality.
Entrapment defense where law enforcement initiated the transaction.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-9-110 covers manufacturing or producing dangerous drugs — possession of precursors with manufacturing intent suffices.
Chemical evidence at the scene establishes manufacturing activity.
Environmental hazards generate aggravating factors.
Co-defendant cooperation testimony often corroborates physical evidence.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the inference of manufacturing from possession of common chemicals.
Argue mere presence at a manufacturing location without participation.
Suppress evidence from warrantless entry.
Challenge expert testimony about whether materials could actually produce the substance.
common_defenses: Innocent possession of chemicals or equipment.
Insufficient evidence to actually produce the substance.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-10-103 covers possession of drug paraphernalia with intent to use.
Residue testing connects paraphernalia to controlled substances.
Proximity to controlled substances strengthens both charges.
Officer testimony about item identification is given significant weight.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether items are actually paraphernalia — many have legitimate uses.
Misdemeanor classification provides minimal exposure.
Argue items belong to another person in shared spaces.
Challenge residue testing reliability.
common_defenses: Legitimate use — tobacco pipe, kitchen scale, etc.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-9-103 covers criminal possession with intent to distribute — felony with substantial penalties.
Distribution intent inferred from quantity, packaging, scales, cash, and communications.
Expert narcotics officer testimony about distribution indicators is highly persuasive.
Possession of multiple drug types or drugs plus firearms strengthens the inference.
defense_opportunities: Challenge intent inference — argue personal use rather than distribution.
Suppress illegally obtained evidence supporting intent.
Contest expert testimony with alternative explanations.
Argue another person was the actual distributor.
common_defenses: Lack of intent — no direct distribution evidence.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-102 (deliberate homicide) is the most serious offense in Montana, carrying potential death penalty or life.
Premeditation evidence (planning, prior threats, weapon acquisition) establishes the deliberate element.
Forensic evidence (DNA, ballistics, digital forensics) provides physical linkage.
Co-defendant cooperation agreements are powerful prosecution tools.
Victim impact testimony admissible at sentencing.
defense_opportunities: Challenge premeditation — argue impulsive killing supporting lesser charges.
Challenge forensic evidence methodology, particularly DNA mixture interpretation.
Alibi defense with independent corroboration.
common_defenses: Lack of premeditation supporting lesser-included offense.

prosecution_strengths: Felony murder doctrine applies to deaths during commission of certain felonies.
Lower mental state requirements than premeditated murder.
Strong forensic and circumstantial evidence typically available.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the mental state — argue accidental or negligent killing.
Heat of passion or extreme emotional disturbance reduces to mitigated deliberate homicide.
Self-defense under Montana's recognized right to defend.
Challenge underlying felony for felony murder cases.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-103 (mitigated deliberate homicide) requires extreme mental or emotional stress.
Prosecution can argue the provocation was insufficient as a matter of law.
Physical evidence of excessive force can undermine the heat-of-passion narrative.
Time delays between provocation and killing defeat the sudden passion defense.
defense_opportunities: This charge is often the defense goal — reducing from deliberate homicide.
Provocation evidence from the victim supports the sudden passion element.
Sentencing range significantly lower than deliberate homicide.
Demonstrate emotional state through 911 calls and post-incident behavior.
common_defenses: Imperfect self-defense — honest but unreasonable belief.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-104 (negligent homicide) requires only negligence — a lower standard than recklessness.
Prosecution does not need to prove intent to kill.
Expert testimony establishing foreseeability of death is often available.
Victim's death creates inherent emotional weight.
defense_opportunities: Argue ordinary negligence rather than criminal negligence — gross deviation standard required.
Challenge causation — intervening factors may have caused the death.
Maximum 20 years but plea negotiations often achievable.
Lack of intent to harm is central to mitigation.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-202 covers purposely or knowingly causing serious bodily injury — up to 20 years.
Medical records documenting serious injuries provide compelling evidence.
Use of a weapon elevates the charge and strengthens the case.
Witness testimony and surveillance footage frequently capture assaults.
defense_opportunities: Mutual combat reduces culpability when both parties willingly engaged in the fight.
Challenge witness identification in chaotic, multi-actor situations where the prosecution cannot pinpoint who delivered the injuring blow.
common_defenses: Lack of intent to cause serious injury.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-201 covers purposely or knowingly causing bodily injury or making insulting/provoking contact.
Even minor injuries or offensive contact satisfies the charge.
Victim and witness testimony often suffices without physical evidence.
Broad statutory language captures diverse conduct.
defense_opportunities: Misdemeanor classification (maximum 6 months) means minimal exposure.
Self-defense applies to all assault charges.
Diversion programs available in many Montana jurisdictions.
Challenge whether contact was truly offensive or injurious.
common_defenses: Consent in sports or mutual contexts.

prosecution_strengths: Even minor physical contact in an offensive manner satisfies the charge.
Victim testimony alone can sustain a conviction.
Broad statutory definition captures wide range of conduct.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense — Montana's broad self-defense rights apply.
Consent — implied consent in athletic or social contexts.
De minimis contact — incidental or trivial contact.
Mistaken identity in crowd situations.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-401 defines robbery as theft with force or threat of force.
Surveillance video commonly captures retail and bank robberies.
Victim identification combined with recovered stolen property is strong.
Cell phone location data and getaway vehicle tracking provide corroboration.
defense_opportunities: Challenge victim identification — stress impairs eyewitness accuracy.
Argue insufficient force to elevate theft to robbery.
Alibi defense with independent corroboration.
Challenge confession voluntariness.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-401 covers robbery with weapons or dangerous instruments, with enhanced penalties.
Even simulated weapons satisfy the element if displayed.
Forensic evidence (fingerprints, DNA, gunshot residue) provides strong physical linkage.
Co-defendant cooperation agreements frequently produce testimony.
defense_opportunities: Challenge whether a weapon was actually displayed.
Identification challenges in traumatic, high-stress situations.
Argue lesser participation than principal actor.
Suppress coerced or suggestive identifications.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-302 covers knowing, unlawful restraint that exposes the victim to risk or interferes with public functions.
Victim testimony about confinement experience is powerful.
Electronic evidence (cell tracking, surveillance) establishes movement and confinement.
Physical evidence at confinement location corroborates the account.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'purpose' element — Montana kidnapping requires specific prohibited purposes.
Argue consent — alleged victim accompanied voluntarily.
Incidental movement during another offense may not constitute separate kidnapping.
Challenge duration and nature of confinement.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-103 covers knowingly starting or causing fires that damage property — felony penalties.
Fire investigation experts determine origin and cause, including accelerant use.
Accelerant detection through laboratory analysis provides physical evidence.
Insurance records and motive evidence support intent.
defense_opportunities: Challenge fire investigator methodology — NFPA 921 standards must be followed.
Argue accidental cause — electrical fault, natural causes, or unintentional ignition.
Challenge accelerant detection — building materials can produce false positives.
Alibi defense for the time the fire started.
common_defenses: False accelerant positive from building materials.

prosecution_strengths: Victim survival allows direct testimony about the attack.
Medical evidence of injuries consistent with lethal intent supports the attempt.
Prior threats and planning evidence establish premeditation.
defense_opportunities: Challenge intent to kill — argue assault rather than attempted murder.
Self-defense under Montana's recognized self-defense rights.
Argue injuries are inconsistent with intent to kill.
Voluntary intoxication may negate specific intent.
common_defenses: Lack of intent to kill — assault rather than attempted murder.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-202(2)(b) covers aggravated assault with a weapon, enhancing penalties significantly.
Physical evidence of the weapon (recovery, DNA, fingerprints) directly links the defendant.
'Weapon' definition is broad and includes any instrument capable of causing death or serious injury.
Victim injuries consistent with weapon use corroborate the charge.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense — defendant armed themselves in response to threat.
Challenge the 'weapon' classification of the object used.
Argue the weapon was present but not used.
Negotiate plea to simple assault by challenging weapon element.
common_defenses: Object does not meet weapon definition.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-301 covers obtaining unauthorized control over property of another with intent to deprive.
Surveillance footage, electronic transaction records, and inventory data provide clear evidence.
Value thresholds determine classification: $1,500+ is a felony.
Witness testimony from victims and employees establishes the taking.
defense_opportunities: Challenge value — under $1,500 is a misdemeanor with significantly lower exposure.
Claim of right — defendant believed entitled to the property.
Identification challenges in retail or crowd settings.
Restitution and diversion programs for first offenders.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-301(3)-(5) makes theft over $1,500 a felony with up to 10 years imprisonment.
Financial records, appraisals, and receipts establish value.
Electronic evidence trails link the defendant to the theft.
Pattern evidence aggregating multiple thefts can reach felony thresholds.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the valuation — fair market value disputes can reduce classification.
Argue authorization or good-faith claim to the property.
Suppress illegally obtained financial or physical evidence.
Negotiate restitution-based resolutions.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-301(2) makes theft under $1,500 a misdemeanor.
Surveillance footage and store employee testimony are typically straightforward.
Repeat offenders face enhanced charges.
Loss prevention officers are trained witnesses.
defense_opportunities: Misdemeanor classification leaves significant room for negotiation.
Diversion programs widely available for first offenders.
Value disputes can affect classification.
Lack of intent defense for absent-mindedness.
common_defenses: Lack of intent — forgot to pay or distracted.

prosecution_strengths: Loss prevention officers document the theft sequence with training and experience.
Store surveillance captures concealment and exit.
Receipt comparison establishes the unpaid items.
Civil recovery statutes allow stores to pursue damages alongside criminal charges.
defense_opportunities: First-offense petty shoplifting carries minimal penalties.
Diversion programs specifically designed for shoplifting cases.
Challenge the stop — loss prevention must observe the entire sequence.
Argue intent to pay — defendant had not yet left the store.
common_defenses: Intent to pay — had not passed last point of sale.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-204 covers knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in an occupied structure with intent to commit an offense.
Physical evidence of forced entry establishes unauthorized entry.
Forensic evidence at the entry point links the defendant.
Surveillance footage and alarm records document timing.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the intent element — entry without proof of intent is trespassing.
Argue authorized entry — permission or apparent permission.
Challenge forensic evidence in spaces with legitimate access.
Lack of forced entry raises authorization questions.
common_defenses: No intent to commit a crime inside.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-204(2) elevates burglary of an occupied dwelling — felony with up to 40 years.
Victim testimony about home invasion is emotionally compelling.
Physical evidence plus stolen property in defendant's possession creates strong circumstantial case.
Home security cameras increasingly capture intruders.
defense_opportunities: Identification challenges if burglar was masked.
Argue dwelling was unoccupied or believed abandoned.
Suppress evidence from illegal searches of defendant's property.
Establish alibi for the time of the burglary.
common_defenses: No intent to commit a crime.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-301(6) makes theft of motor vehicles an automatic felony regardless of value.
Vehicle identification through VIN, registration, and GPS makes the stolen vehicle easy to identify.
Possession of recently stolen vehicle creates a presumption of knowledge.
Surveillance footage tracks vehicle movement.
defense_opportunities: Argue permission from owner or reasonable belief of permission.
Challenge the 'taking' element — passenger status is not theft.
Joyriding/temporary use defense.
Identification challenges.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge that vehicle was stolen.
Temporary use without intent to permanently deprive.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-301(12) covers receiving or possessing stolen property with knowledge.
Circumstances of acquisition (suspiciously low price, no documentation) support knowledge inference.
Serial numbers and victim identification establish stolen status.
Electronic records can show defendant knew the property was stolen.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the knowledge element — good-faith purchase defense.
Argue purchase price was favorable but not suspiciously low.
Challenge whether property was actually stolen.
Lack of proof that property is the specific stolen item.
common_defenses: Innocent receipt as gift or legitimate transaction.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-101 (criminal mischief) covers knowingly damaging property of another.
Surveillance footage, witness testimony, and physical evidence link the defendant.
Damage estimates from professionals establish financial impact.
Social media admissions are often available.
defense_opportunities: Challenge value of damage to affect classification.
Argue accidental damage — not 'knowingly' caused.
Claim of ownership — defendant believed they could alter the property.
Restitution-based resolution often available.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-203 (criminal trespass) covers knowingly entering or remaining on property without privilege.
Posted signs, fences, and verbal warnings establish off-limits status.
Surveillance footage and witness testimony are direct evidence.
Prior trespass warnings establish knowledge for repeat offenders.
defense_opportunities: Misdemeanor classification provides room for alternative resolution.
Argue lack of knowledge of private property status.
Challenge whether proper notice was given.
Assert legal right to be on property.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-101 broadly covers damaging, tampering with, or destroying property.
Specific tampering acts (cutting wires, puncturing tires) clearly demonstrate intent.
Motive evidence from disputes provides context.
Pattern of incidents strengthens the case.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'knowingly' element.
Argue ownership or shared interest in the property.
Misdemeanor classification for first offense.
Restitution agreement supports resolution.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-206 (partner or family member assault) carries enhanced penalties for domestic relationship.
Victim statements as excited utterances are admissible even if recanted.
Physical evidence (injuries, damaged property, 911 recording) corroborates initial accounts.
Mandatory arrest policy ensures cases enter the system.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense — defendant was the victim of initial aggression.
Recantation can create reasonable doubt.
Challenge the 'partner or family member' definition.
Mutual combat defense.
common_defenses: False accusation tied to custody or divorce.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-206(1)(a) specifically covers causing bodily injury to a partner or family member.
Even minor physical contact in domestic context satisfies the offense.
Bodycam footage of the scene is compelling evidence.
Prior domestic violence history may be admissible.
defense_opportunities: Misdemeanor for first offense provides room for diversion.
Self-defense applies fully.
Challenge the offensive contact threshold.
Counseling programs in lieu of prosecution.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-628 covers endangering the welfare of a child by knowingly creating risk.
Mandated reporter testimony is credible and specific.
Environmental evidence documents endangerment.
Children's statements to forensic interviewers may be admissible.
defense_opportunities: Challenge the 'substantial risk' standard.
Cultural and lifestyle differences should not be criminalized.
Temporary conditions being addressed mitigate the charge.
Constitutional parental rights arguments.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge of dangerous condition.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-212 covers knowingly causing or permitting injury to a child.
Medical evidence of inflicted injuries (fracture patterns, multiple injuries) is highly persuasive.
Pediatric expert testimony distinguishes accidental from inflicted injuries.
Child forensic interview statements are often admissible.
defense_opportunities: Challenge medical evidence — injuries consistent with accidents.
Identify alternative perpetrator with access to child.
Reasonable discipline defense (within limits).
Medical condition defense (osteogenesis imperfecta, bleeding disorders).

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-626 makes violation of an order of protection criminal with escalating repeat penalties.
The protective order itself establishes prohibited conduct.
Electronic evidence frequently proves violations.
Service records confirm defendant's awareness.
defense_opportunities: Challenge service of the order.
Argue contact was initiated by the protected party.
Challenge scope of the order — actions may not violate specific terms.
Constitutional challenges to overbroad provisions.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-220 covers purposely or knowingly causing reasonable apprehension or substantial emotional distress.
Pattern evidence from multiple incidents establishes course of conduct.
Electronic evidence creates detailed records.
Victim testimony about psychological impact is compelling.
defense_opportunities: Challenge course of conduct — isolated incidents may not suffice.
Constitutionally protected activity defense.
Challenge reasonable apprehension standard.
Demonstrate legitimate purpose for contact.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-5-201 includes physical contact intended to insult or provoke.
Electronic communication records provide documented patterns.
Multiple witnesses corroborate harassing behavior.
Prior warnings establish defendant's awareness.
defense_opportunities: Misdemeanor classification provides room for alternative resolution.
Argue legitimate purpose for communications.
Free speech defense.
Challenge whether conduct rises to harassment level.

prosecution_strengths: Section 52-3-825 covers physical, emotional, or financial exploitation of vulnerable adults.
Medical evidence of injuries or neglect is compelling.
Financial records document exploitation.
Adult Protective Services investigations provide credible testimony.
defense_opportunities: Challenge causation of injuries — falls, medical conditions, medications.
Argue authorization for financial transactions.
Distinguish imperfect care from criminal abuse.
Power of attorney authorization defense.
common_defenses: Lack of intent to cause injury.
Caregiver doing best with available resources.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-8-316 covers carrying concealed weapons in certain circumstances or by prohibited persons.
Physical recovery of the weapon is direct evidence.
Witness testimony about display or use is strong.
Location-based violations are straightforward.
defense_opportunities: Montana has strong Second Amendment protections and permissive concealed carry laws.
Challenge whether the location triggered a violation.
Constitutional challenges to specific restrictions.
Argue lack of knowledge of weapon's presence.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-8-313 prohibits felons from possessing firearms — straightforward elements.
Prior felony conviction is documented and difficult to challenge.
Physical recovery plus forensic evidence links the weapon.
Constructive possession can suffice.
defense_opportunities: Challenge constructive possession in shared spaces.
Argue lack of knowledge of weapon's presence.
Challenge underlying felony conviction if constitutionally deficient.
Temporary, innocent possession defense.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-8-328 covers certain concealed carry violations despite Montana's permissive laws.
Physical recovery and circumstance evidence is straightforward.
Officer testimony about discovery is direct.
Video evidence from restricted locations supports the charge.
defense_opportunities: Montana's permissive concealed carry laws significantly narrowed criminal exposure.
Challenge whether the location is actually restricted.
Argue lack of knowledge of restricted zone.
Improper stop or search.
common_defenses: Lack of knowledge of restricted zone.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-8-111 makes discharging a firearm in certain locations or circumstances criminal.
Physical evidence (shell casings, bullet impacts, gunshot residue) links the defendant.
Witness testimony and surveillance footage are direct evidence.
Ballistic comparison provides forensic linkage.
defense_opportunities: Self-defense.
Lawful discharge on private property.
Accidental discharge.
Challenge identification.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-332 covers obtaining or using personal identifying information without authorization.
Digital evidence trails trace fraudulent activity to the defendant.
Financial records document unauthorized transactions.
Victim testimony establishes harm.
defense_opportunities: Challenge digital evidence attribution.
Argue authorization from identity holder.
Challenge chain of custody for digital evidence.
Mistaken attribution defense.

prosecution_strengths: Financial records and accounting analysis trace the misappropriation.
Forensic accounting identifies unauthorized transactions.
Internal witnesses provide credible testimony.
defense_opportunities: Argue authorization for transactions.
Challenge forensic accounting methodology.
Argue lack of intent to permanently deprive.
Challenge valuation.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-325 covers making, completing, or altering documents with intent to defraud.
Document examination experts identify forged signatures and alterations.
Handwriting comparison provides forensic evidence.
The forged document itself is direct evidence.
defense_opportunities: Argue authorization to sign.
Challenge document examiner methodology.
Argue lack of fraudulent intent.
Identity defense.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-326 covers counterfeiting and possession of counterfeiting equipment.
Physical evidence at defendant's location is strong.
Federal-state cooperation brings Secret Service resources.
Passing counterfeit items is documented through victim and surveillance evidence.
defense_opportunities: Argue lack of knowledge of counterfeit nature.
Challenge the search.
Argue legitimate purpose for materials (art, props).
Distinguish possession from production.

prosecution_strengths: Section 45-6-316 covers issuing bad checks knowing of insufficient funds.
Bank records document insufficient funds at time of issuance.
The check itself is physical evidence.
Notice of dishonor and failure to make good creates a presumption of knowledge.
defense_opportunities: Argue good-faith belief that funds were available.
Challenge timing — funds deposited before presentment.
Restitution within statutory period as defense.
Post-dated check defense.
common_defenses: Good faith belief in sufficient funds.

prosecution_strengths: Section 33-1-1202 makes insurance fraud a felony covering false claims and statements to insurers.
Insurance company SIU units compile comprehensive evidence packages.
Surveillance footage contradicting claims is powerful.
